Peridot serves a menu of fermentation-forward, plant-based cocktails and fare to guests on the 38th floor of The Henderson building, which completed in 2024. At Peridot, thousands of tiny lights dot the curved walls and ceiling Studio Paolo Ferrari approached the space in a style its founder describes as "timeless futurism", and the result is a cocoon-like interior enveloped almost entirely in lime green. "We wanted the space to embody the energy and dynamism of Hong Kong, a space rooted in the elegance of the past, but propelled by possibility," said Ferrari. Green marble forms the service counter and a mirrored ceiling reflects the liquor bottle display behind The bar interior's continuously curved walls and ceiling are dotted with over 20,000 tiny lights that shine through protruding frosted acrylic cylinders. The effect of these pixel-like elements is akin to an exploded disco ball, and the surrealism is intensified by the all-green decor and its reflective surfaces. "There's a sense of infinite expansion, but it's deeply personal, abstract, yet strangely familiar," said Ferrari. A marble-lined passage leads to a hidden lounge Echoing the architecture, sculptural sinuous walls frame large windows that overlook the Hong Kong skyline, which guests can enjoy from curvaceous mohair-upholstered sofas and lounge chairs. The service counter sits within another framed arch, almost like a theatrical stage, and is made from green marble that extends across the adjacent walls and spills onto the floor. The effect of the tiny lights is even more impactful inside the windowless lounge A mirrored ceiling reflects the illuminated back bottle display and the cocktail servers preparing drinks in front. "Familiar forms are abstracted, noble materials are reframed, and the result is a space that invites both reflection and projection," Ferrari said. "This is Timeless Futurism: memory in dialogue with courageous invention." Curvaceous sofas are tucked into alcoves, and the lights reflect off s

Located within a heritage-listed building that was constructed in 1897 as the Jones and Higgins department store, the Peckham Palais nightclub was revamped after being vacant for nearly 15 years. Nikjoo and Fare Inc renovated the Peckham Palais nightclub Working for Nightlife specialist Night Group , architecture studio Nikjoo was responsible for adapting the derelict building into a multi-room cultural destination that reached modern acoustic and fire safety requirements. Fare Inc oversaw the interior design, layouts, finishes and furnishings, which aim to retain a sense of the building's evolution while evoking the period when the original Palais nightclub was established in 1980. A first floor bar has a refined sense of style "Our approach was not to erase what had come before, but to work with it, to preserve the details people feel connected to and allow the building's history to remain visible," said Fare Inc founder Annie Harrison. "We wanted Palais to feel like it had always been here; layered, atmospheric and alive again." Chipped paint was left on the stairs Customers enter the building through a lobby and box office on the ground floor, where peeling plaster and chipped paint enhance the sense of faded glamour. The main venue is in the basement. In contrast to the lobby's rough-and-ready aesthetic, the first-floor Ballroom bar displays a more refined sense of style informed by 1980s interiors. "We explored a tonal yet layered design to ensure there was a polished look to the rooms," Harrison told Dezeen. "[The materials] "seem to have always been there, which makes them feel discovered rather than added." Graffiti was left on the windows The 270-capacity cocktail bar features deep-raspberry coloured walls, along with banquettes upholstered in leather and PVC that contribute to the warm and playful atmosphere. The spacious eatery is housed within a nineteenth-century gothic building, which features double-height ceilings and an expansive glass facade with intricate detailing. The design was informed by traditional Parisian bistros Located in Covent Garden, the restaurant spans 107 square metres and accommodates 52 customers across a ground floor dining room and a basement level. An outdoor terrace welcomes an additional 30 guests when the weather permits. "Our brief talked about a neighbourhood restaurant in the centre of town," Gundry & Ducker co-founder Tyeth Gundry told Dezeen. "From there, the conversation centred on familiarity, recognition and ease – creating a neighbourhood restaurant for friends who live in different parts of the city." The studio chose a warm, neutral colour palette for the interior The studio intended for the design to resemble traditional Parisian establishments by incorporating familiar elements, including deep aubergine finishes, dark banquette seating and classic bentwood bistro chairs. Alongside this, the designers combined natural fabrics, sapele wood and stainless steel with exposed brickwork to create a restrained colour palette and an overall "deliberately unfussy" interior. The design combines a mixture of dark woods with natural fabrics and stainless steel "We talked a lot about colour: summer park landscapes, Parisian bistros and wine," Gundry explained. "Tone too was really important; we needed colours that would dim well to help us create a low-level evening setting that feels warm; the key to which is controlling reflected light," he continued. The Grade II-listed interior has double-height ceilings and a large glass facade Taking cues from the surrounding theatre district, the studio installed a sophisticated sound system and a statement curtain with acoustic qualities that wraps around the main dining area. items.title: Ten pandemic-era dining sheds that show "wildly different tastes" of New Yorkers
items.text: Ten pandemic-era dining sheds that show "wildly different tastes" of New Yorkers Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Ten pandemic-era dining sheds that show "wildly different tastes" of New Yorkers Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Ben Dreith | 11 October 2026 From hastily installed sheds and tents to more intricate structures with signage and considered design, author Penny Hardy highlights the absurdity, delight and ingenuity of dining sheds installed in New York during the Covid-19 pandemic . Collected in Hardy's recently announced book, Pandemic Architecture: NYC Dining Sheds 2020-2024 , the sheds represent a very specific time in the landscape of the city, when restaurants tried to operate during indoor dining restrictions. Many have since been deconstructed, as the city tries to implement a standardised shed programme to keep the seating while maintaining safety and sanitation standards. New York mayor Zohran Mamdani recently cleared the legal way for year-round installation . Hardy took photos of the sheds in Downtown Manhattan on walks during the height of the pandemic and afterwards, as many remained up for years after the 2020 to 2021 lockdowns. Though many of the restaurants have since closed or moved, Hardy believes that it's clear that the impact of the structures has changed the way we view the streetscape. Penny Hardy's new book looks at the range of impromptu dining sheds installed in New York during the Covid-19 pandemic "These structures created a new typology for building in public space and have forever changed the way we use the street," she told Dezeen. "Before this new typology, the street was aggressively preserved as a place of transit by the city. Now, in addition to transit, it offers a place for people to connect and socialise." She added that the recent city legislation opens up room for a return to the creativity that has been limited by the high costs of storage and assembly of the structures during the winter months. "The restaurant owners' resourcefulness, humour, and wildly different tastes made the streets more varied and alive," said Hardy. "The structures were raw, inventive, funny, and as varied as New York itself. They brought an old-school punk, DIY spirit back into an increasingly polished city." Located in the city's Escandón I neighbourhood, Nota Tavern is a two-storey Italian-American restaurant. It sits on a site that once held a hacienda-style residence that was converted into an apartment building, with the owner preserving half of the original house. The restaurant sits in this portion. Formant Studio designed the interiors and most of the furniture at Nota Tavern in Mexico City Formant Studio was tasked with translating the design of classic Chicago taverns into a contemporary mode. "The main request was to create a faithful interpretation of the neighbourhood taverns of Chicago – the kind of places built less around spectacle and more around familiarity," Formant Studio co-founder Alejandro Valencia told Dezeen. "The design translates the character of a classic tavern into a contemporary architectural language." The two-storey restaurant serves Italian-American cuisine Valencia also said the studio took other cues from Chicago and integrated the clean minimalism of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and the warmer modernism of Frank Lloyd Wright , both architects known for their work in the US city. Also in the tradition of the 20th-century modern architects, Formant Studio designed most of the furniture, from the black-stained oak tables to the steel bar stools and sleek metal sconces. The space was once a hacienda-style residence and its original columns were preserved and restored The majority of the dining room was clad in Mexican rosewood panels, which also form the custom banquettes upholstered in black Kvadrat textiles. Formant Studio said that the previous space defined how it organised the restaurant. Mexican rosewood covers the walls and forms banquette seating The current space still has ornate stone pillars that once framed an entrance portico. items.text: Spirit of Iberian taverns informs wood-heavy Parisian restaurant Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Spirit of Iberian taverns informs wood-heavy Parisian restaurant Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Jane Englefield | 6 October 2026 Emerging Marseille firm Bétyle Studio has designed the interiors for Arcane 17, a Basque and Catalan restaurant in Paris featuring patinated timber and distinctive marquetry . Located in the city's Le Marais neighbourhood in the 4th arrondissement, Arcane 17 is a petite eatery that sits within a centuries-old building. Arcane 17 is a Basque and Catalan restaurant Bétyle Studio founders Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche wanted to honour the owners' Catalan roots through their restaurant design. "Rather than reproducing the codes of a traditional Spanish restaurant, we wanted to reinterpret the idea of the Iberian tavern through a more contemporary and refined language," studio founders Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche told Dezeen. Bétyle Studio designed the interiors for the space In this spirit, the designers clad the open space in an abundance of wood. The dining area is characterised by ebonised panelling, while the tubular stainless steel bar is topped with delicate slabs of marquetry detailing playful motifs, from shooting stars to a cartoonish lobster. Classic bentwood chairs make up the dining space "We drew inspiration from the energy of rural churches, dark woods and the movement of traditional fans," explained Romano and Cazenave de la Roche. "We did not want these references to be literal, but rather to emerge through materials, textures and forms." Classic, bentwood chairs feature alongside uniform timber tables. In one corner, a red-clad banquette subtly nods to traditional Parisian bistros. Read: Gjergji Shkurti integrates bar, retail and hi-fi at Million Goods in Brooklyn All of the space's joinery was conceived bespoke for the restaurant by a Marseille-based carpenter and frequent collaborator of Bétyle Studio. "We worked with different species of wood and experimented with various techniques to stain, ebonise and patinate the timber," said Romano and Cazenave de la Roche. "The idea was to give depth to the surfaces and create elements that feel as though they could have belonged to the space for a long time." items.text: Bar Shrimp uses laser-etched acoustic panels to balance music and conversation Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Bar Shrimp uses laser-etched acoustic panels to balance music and conversation Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Francesca Tesler | 6 October 2026 Cocktail bar and restaurant Bar Shrimp combines red velvet interiors with bespoke acoustic panels from Autex Acoustics to balance music and conversation, shown in this video produced by Dezeen. Located in Manchester , Bar Shrimp has a custom sound system and a dark interior with floor-to-ceiling red velvet curtains and plush banquettes, reminiscent of vintage New York bars and music lounges. The design was informed by the founders' experience of bars around the world, where co-founder Richard Cossins said they were struck by ones with particularly good sound. "When we first saw the space, we wanted to create a relaxed and comfortable environment, where guests could spend numerous hours within the space," Cossins told Dezeen. Bar Shrimp's interior draws on mid-century bar decor The existing space had a concrete floor and glass walls, prompting the team to introduce softer materials to improve the acoustics. Autex Acoustics worked with the team from an early stage, supplying a bespoke Frontier Axis ceiling system and Mirage wall panels to reduce reverberation and echo. The acoustic treatment was designed to complement the interior rather than disappear into it, with laser-etched patterns giving the Mirage panels a textured finish inspired by natural materials. DJs provide a curated music programme throughout the day "We're looking at it from a technical perspective, but also from an aesthetic perspective," said Autex Acoustics UK, EU and the Middle East director Daniel Senior. "We laser etch a pattern into a panel," he continued. "That allows us to create some really intricate designs, to create real depth and texture to a panel, all taking inspiration from natural materials." Bar Shrimp also features a custom MasterSounds Clarity M-1215 Audio system – a large-format modular speaker system designed to provide high-quality sound throughout the space. The panels were chosen to blend with the rest of the restaurant's interior. Cossins said the acoustic treatment was intended to make the bar comfortable even when music is playing at a high volume. Hommali is located at the edges of New York's West Village neighbourhood and was founded by Bangkok natives chef Chattchakorn "Benz" Khajornchaisan, general manager Kritayanee "Air" Promsarin and operations lead Pichalak "Picha" Srigungvarl after they moved to New York City and met in the hospitality scene. Surrane Design has completed a Thai restaurant in the West Village The restaurant contains an eight-seat bar, a 20-seat dining den, a semi-private mezzanine and auxiliary spaces such as a wine room and dry-age room where ducks and other ferments are on display. Surrane Design layered the space with a rich assortment of textures and patterns, such as dark wood millwork, a marbled bar top and artwork sourced from Bangkok's Chatuchak Weekend Market. It brings together a rich assortment of textures and colours informed by Thailand According to the team, its palette of browns and greens was informed by the life cycle of a rice plant. "The color palette is inspired by the stages of the rice plant: fresh green for young leaves, golden yellow for mature stalks, earthy brown for paddy soil, soft beige for rice husks, and warm cream white for polished rice," said the team. Personal items from the ownership team line a partition It was designed to resemble a traditional Thai house, where the central dining den and mezzanine above recall a courtyard, and the terracotta floor also calls to the vernacular architecture of the country. Visitors are greeted with a rice plant light installation at the doorway and enter by the bar, which is clad in a sandy fluted tile with seats upholstered in leather and velvet. Stairs lead to a mezzanine with additional seating Two booths sit in front of the main dining space, which is tucked beneath the mezzanine. Curtains and open shelving separate the two spaces. items.text: Montreal restaurant Minnibar by Ivy Studio "embraces its raw shell" Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Montreal restaurant Minnibar by Ivy Studio "embraces its raw shell" Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Dan Howarth | 1 August 2026 Japanese minimalism has informed the interiors of this light-filled Italian restaurant in Montreal , designed by locally based Ivy Studio with its first in-house designed chairs. Located on the ground level of a Downtown high-rise residential tower, Minnibar utilises the 20-foot (6-metre) ceilings, corner aspect and almost square floor plan to its advantage. At the entrance to Minnibar, a pale stone-clad cafe counter drops in height to become an omakase-style ledge Ivy Studio left the building's structure entirely visible, and only added elements where functionally necessary – using the principles of Japanese minimalism as a guide. "Minnibar embraces its raw shell," said the studio. "Exposed base-building elements – including the naturally sealed concrete floor, formidable concrete columns, walls, and the ceiling slab – are left untouched." A slender black ledge along the windows provides space for dining The kitchen, bar and pizza counter are housed within an enclosed central core, allowing the cafe and restaurant spaces to flow openly around the perimeter. Morning patrons have easy access from the entrance to the cafe counter, which is clad in monolithic, cream-colored stone with a leather finish. Triangular shapes can be spotted in the wall-mounted lighting and millwork details As it continues into the space, the counter drops in height and is replaced with an omakase-style ledge crafted from white oak. Opposite, a black shelf runs along the windows to provide additional bar dining space, accompanied by circular white stools. The main dining area is arranged symmetrically around glowing wall-mounted artwork "The design employs a strict monochromatic palette, playing with off-white and grey shades punctuated by sharp black integrations," said Ivy Studio. "To give the minimalist aesthetic a profound sense of depth, the design introduces subtle, highly tactile finishes: hand-plastered walls, heavily textured stones, opaque stained wood grains, and translucent textiles." items.title: Stone and lace details "evoke the atmosphere of Cyprus" at London restaurant Zylia
items.text: Stone and lace details "evoke the atmosphere of Cyprus" at Zylia Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Stone and lace details "evoke the atmosphere of Cyprus" at London restaurant Zylia Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Cajsa Carlson | 24 July 2026 Architecture studio Red Deer sourced Gerolakkos stone and hand-crafted Lefkara lace from Cyprus, which it juxtaposed with stainless steel and oversized basket-like lamps at Zylia in Covent Garden. The design of the restaurant, which serves food inspired by Greek Cypriot cooking, was adapted to suit the old factory building in which it's located and reference the provenance of its menu. "We wanted to introduce a distinctly Cypriot sensibility into the existing shell, a former Victorian blacking factory in Covent Garden," Red Deer founding director Lionel Real de Azúa told Dezeen. "The design became an exercise in dialogue rather than imitation, allowing materials, textures and references from Cyprus to inhabit an unmistakably London industrial building." Zylia is a Greek Cypriot restaurant in Covent Garden After a trip to Cyprus together with Zylia co-founder Barry Karacostas, Real de Azúa decided that the island country's Gerolakkos stone would be one of the features of the restaurant. "One of the defining materials is Gerolakkos stone, or pouropetra, the warm honey-coloured limestone found throughout Cyprus and used for centuries in everything from civic buildings to humble garden walls," he said. "The slabs used on the main counter and waiter stations were quarried and shipped directly from Cyprus, arriving only days before completion." Stainless-steel tables are juxtaposed with craft details The tactile stone slabs were contrasted with stainless-steel finishes, which were used on the tabletops and chair legs. "The contrast is important. Rather than allowing one material to dominate the other, the project relies on the tension between them," Real de Azúa said. As well as the solid materials, Red Deer also drew on Cyprus' tradition of handcrafts when creating the interior, which features local lace and woven pendant lights that add a homely feel. items.text: Louvre walls enclose restaurant in Thailand by Studio Locomotive Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Breezy louvre walls enclose restaurant in Thailand by Studio Locomotive Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Jon Astbury | 22 July 2026 An external skin of timber louvres filters light and air into the double-height interiors of Waankarn, a restaurant and events space in Thailand designed by local architecture practice Studio Locomotive . Located in the coastal village of Khao Lak, the space was designed to combine a bar and restaurant for the area's increasing number of tourists, with spaces that can be used by the local community for gatherings and exhibitions. Studio Locomotive has completed a restaurant and events space in Thailand According to Studio Locomotive , its use of vernacular materials and techniques was a means of allowing visitors to "experience the sensory realities of Southern Thai living", most notably through the breezy walls of louvres made from Ceylon ironwood. "We approached the context as a living condition, allowing guests to intuitively feel how localised structures breathe and function," Thanart Chanyu, design director at Studio Locomotive, told Dezeen. Timber louvres filter light and air into the interiors "We translated this into an evocative spatial character, managing the tropical climate through strategic architectural apertures, tactile woodwork, and the moisture radiating from earth-bound masonry," he added. Waankarn's louvre walls wrap two double-height spaces on either side of a wide, stepped concrete corridor, which was designed to double as a space for temporary exhibitions organised by the community. A concrete corridor doubles as an exhibition space To the north of this corridor is the main dining room and to the south a smaller bar space, both of which are defined by walls of timber louvres and exposed concrete, skylit ceilings and granite floors. This simple palette was complemented by the use of repurposed materials, which, according to Studio Locomotive, were a means of creating a "cultural bridge" for visitors less familiar with the area. In the bar, a countertop was made from a five-centimetre-thick sheet of salvaged industrial steel, which sits in front of a large feature wall created by repurposing a section of local, traditional clay tile roof. items.title: Tokyo's drinking alleys inform interior of Genso restaurant by Joyce Wang Studio
items.text: Tokyo's drinking alleys inform Genso restaurant by Joyce Wang Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Tokyo's drinking alleys inform interior of Genso restaurant by Joyce Wang Studio Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Natasha Levy | 21 July 2026 Lanterns, alley-like walkways and other details reminiscent of Tokyo's Golden Gai neighbourhood feature in this restaurant designed by Joyce Wang Studio in Hong Kong . Genso is one of several dining options at Hong Kong's Sha Tin Racecourse , which opened in 1978 to cater to the city's growing demand for horse races. The two-floor restaurant offers a variety of Japanese fare, and its interiors take inspiration from Japan, too – most notably Golden Gai, a buzzy pocket of Tokyo's Shinjuku ward known for its grid of narrow alleyways packed with tiny bars and eateries. A tiled counter marks the entrance to Genso restaurant "Golden Gai is a city within a city; it has its own rules, its own personality, it really feels like you can escape and lose yourself within it," designer Joyce Wang told Dezeen. "For Genso, we wanted to recreate that feeling and carve out different levels and layers to the space – in the form of stairs, platforms, bridges, lookouts, walkways – capturing the diverse experiences that exist in a vibrant city like Tokyo, and Hong Kong." Upholstered banquettes and lanterns feature in the casual dining space downstairs At the front of the restaurant stands a large reception desk. Its base is inky-blue stained timber while the counter is clad with tiny ceramic tiles, evocative of pixelated manga styles or old-school video games. For Wang, it was important that Genso had a slightly retro feel. "There's something appealing about a time that is difficult to pinpoint and place; it feels less clearly defined, which allows it to resonate across generations," she explained. Tile inlays emulate the ceramic facades of Tokyo buildings After guests pass the desk, they come to the restaurant's lower level, Fudo Town Food Hall, where Japanese street food is served. The space is designed to have a casual atmosphere, with a series of open booths and long communal banquettes, upholstered in blue leather and patterned orange fabric. Walkways and steps lead to the restaurant's second floor Some of the tables and structural columns were inlaid with blue tiles in a subtle nod to the ceramic building facades often seen throughout Tokyo. items.title: OMA's Oberon restaurant at the New Museum is "hidden in plain sight"
items.text: OMA's Oberon restaurant at the New Museum hides "in plain sight" Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats OMA's Oberon restaurant at the New Museum is "hidden in plain sight" Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Dan Howarth | 18 July 2026 Architecture studio OMA has designed a "jewel box" restaurant clad in cork inside its recently completed extension to the New Museum in Manhattan. All-day bar and restaurant Oberon has opened a few months after the expansion, which OMA New York completed adjacent to the original SANAA-designed building. Oberon appears as a metallic box within the ground-floor lobby of the expanded New Museum Sitting adjacent to the lobby, in the expansion's ground floor, the 2,500-square-foot (230-square-metre) restaurant appears as a metallic box with a single horizontal band of frosted glass wrapping its exterior, hinting at what's inside. It was clad in cork that was then painted a silver colour, blending it into the industrial materials of the museum s[ace "'Hidden-in-plain-sight,' the restaurant resembles a jewel box or an inverted white cube gallery," said OMA. The restaurant can be entered from the museum lobby or a separate entrance on Freemans Alley The studio's first restaurant design in the US, Oberon is accessible directly from the museum lobby as well as a separate, speakeasy-style entrance from Freeman Alley. "We imagined the restaurant both as part of, and independent from the museum," said OMA New York partner Shohei Shigematsu. "Conceived as a freestanding box inserted into the ground-floor lobby, it will be accessible from the building's front and back, day to night." The moody, cavernous restaurant interior contrasts the bright industrial museum The interior's moody, cavernous aesthetic is a stark contrast to the museum's industrial concrete and metal lobby and galleries. "Inside, a large dining room and fixed pockets of seating will offer space to gather or retreat," said Shigematsu. "Organic, tactile material finishes complementing the museum's polished lightness, will introduce a warm and comforting environment that eases people in and invites them to stay." Booth seating and ceilings are made entirely from black expanded cork, while pendant lights are by Minjae Kim Over the central dining area, filled with freestanding wooden tables and chairs, the cork ceiling is carved away to create an elongated dome ringed with cove lighting. items.text: Open Studio designs izakaya-style restaurant with dumpling lamp Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Open Studio designs izakaya-style restaurant with "half-dipped dumpling" lamp Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Cajsa Carlson | 2 July 2026 Local firm Open Studio has created a gigantic fibreglass dumpling to illuminate and beckon visitors into Dumpling Darlings, a small-plates restaurant in Singapore 's New Bahru shopping centre. The studio looked to traditional Japanese izakayas when designing the restaurant for New Bahru, a dining and shopping location in an old, breeze-block-clad modernist school . Dumpling Darlings is located at the New Bahru shopping centre "These izakaya very often spill out onto the street, and are recognisable for their compact seating tucked beneath low retractable eaves," Jax Tan, who co-founded Open Studio with Lam Jun Nan, told Dezeen. "That blurred boundary between the street and the restaurant is what we found most interesting and sought to interpret for Dumpling Darlings." It was designed by Open Studio with an izakaya-style roof This inspiration can mainly be seen in the design of Dumpling Darlings ' roof, which is made from corrugated perforated steel in a dark red hue and sits low over the front of the 100-square-metre restaurant. "The lightweight roof became our primary architectural gesture, angled low to create the sense of roadside enclosure while defining the shopfront," Tan said. "Our goal was to capture the feeling of being at the izakaya, rather than the look of one." A "half-dipped" dumpling lamp peeks through the roof A gigantic, pale-red dumpling lamp hangs from the ceiling and peeps through the izakaya's roof to illuminate the restaurant's outdoor seating space and tempt customers craving dumplings. "In traditional izakayas, traditional Japanese akachōchin, red paper lanterns, are hung outside as welcome signs," Tan explained. Read: FARM and Nice Projects turn breeze-block-clad modernist school into lifestyle hub "We didn't reproduce the lantern literally, but imagined that the dumpling could be a similar beacon beckoning dumpling seekers," she continued. "The oversized fibreglass dumpling is half dipped into a roof cut-out, providing a moment of levity against an otherwise disciplined tectonic interior." A Listening Bar Where Yugoslav Modernism Meets Japanese Hi-Fi Culture Supaform’s interiors for EJE incorporate his furniture and art, plus original London Underground textiles, vintage speaker systems, and more. Photos: Varvara Toplennikova Had you visited Yugoslavia in the 1970s, you would have seen thousands of modular structures dotting the streets, instantly recognizable by their rounded, space-age exteriors and large central picture windows. Expandable to encompass anything from newspaper stands to copy shops to small cafes, these were the iconic K67 kiosks, envisioned by the Slavic architect and industrial designer Saša J. Mächtig in 1966 and now altogether more rare in the country. It was these stands — along with Yugoslav brutalism and futurism in general, plus the aesthetic and sound design of Japanese listening bars, that inspired the interiors of Esthetic Joys Embassy, or EJE , in Belgrade. Comprising a bar, a restaurant, a DJ booth, a vinyl library with listening stations, and a dance floor that’s attached to a hotel, EJE was designed by Supaform , and features not only principal Maxim Scherbakov’s furniture designs but his artworks as well, as seen in the lower right photo above. Other key details include a pair of vintage JBL 4435 studio monitors, an iconic Japanese train station clock called the Dulton Double Face, and archival Mischa Black upholstery fabric — used on the London Tube in the 1970s — that Scherbakov’s team sourced from the original London mill that made it. The idea, he says, was to transform the space into a utopia that inspired both nostalgia and optimism; “a futuristic, autonomous station of aesthetic pleasures.” One of Athens’s Great Midcentury Landmarks Enters a New Era At top, a suite at the newly renovated Conrad Athens the Ilisian; bottom, its original 1963 facade and a shot from its Yabu Pushelberg–designe

Art and Architecture Find a Perfect Dialogue Inside a Modernist Connecticut Landmark Artworks made from paper layered on top of linen canvases by Kim Bartelt, on view through tomorrow at the 1960 John Landis–designed Gores Pavilion in Connecticut. One downside of taking an annual summer break from our newsletter: We sometimes miss the window for exhibitions and other time-sensitive projects. This site-specific exhibition of new work by Berlin artist Kim Bartelt is only on view until the end of the day tomorrow, but assuming most of you aren’t anywhere near New Canaan, Connecticut, anyway, we figured we might as well enable you to enjoy it from afar. For “Exhibit No. 2,” presented by Arden + White Gallery , Bartelt installed 8 of her understated-yet-colorful paper-and-linen compositions inside the Gores Pavilion , a landmarked home designed by modernist architect — and Philip Johnson collaborator — Landis Gores in 1960. The artworks resonate with both the colors and the geometries found in the home, but they weren’t so much inspired by the architecture as chosen to complement it; if you know Bartelt’s work, you know this has been her visual language for years. As the gallery puts it: “This exhibition is not about illustrating architecture, nor about placing contemporary art within an iconic building. Rather, it reveals a shared architectural sensibility, one rooted in proportion, restraint, and the thoughtful orchestration of material, light, and space.” Walker Street Market Is Turning the Berkshires Into a Contemporary Design Destination At Walker Street Market in Lenox, Mass., the craft-forward fare includes a custom counter by Brian Persico and painting by David Silverstein (top), a side table by Simone Bodmer Turner and lamp by Ashley Joseph Martin (above left), and a teapot by Akira Satake (above right), among many others. For a Summer, the Athens-Based Gallery Antiqua is Trading White Walls for the Deep Blue Sea The Athens-based 20th-century furniture gallery Antiqua is popping up on the Greek island of Antiparos for the summer in a show called “By the Sea.” Photos: Giorgos Sfakianakis One regrettable limitation of having a permanent gallery space is that, regardless of how much exhibition design you can pull off, or how many bizarre interventions ensue, each show still retains the DNA of its enclosure. An Alex Da Corte show at Karma Gallery — even with red carpeting, pink walls, and an upside-down inflatable cat — still feels like a typical Karma Gallery show; heavy curtains or a Do Ho Suh–esque house can’t fool you into thinking you’re not at Jacqueline Sullivan’s. (Perhaps the most successful transformation of a known space I’ve ever seen was Felix Burrichter’s Charlap Hyman & Herrero–designed BLOW-UP exhibition for Friedman Benda , but that’s another story for another day about how 2019 was my favorite year in design.) This is why it’s so exciting when a shop or gallery decides to decamp entirely to a new space, whether for the long haul or even for a few months. There’s a pleasant friction that develops from seeing the same pieces in a new envelope. The Athens-based 20th-century furniture gallery Antiqua is taking full advantage of that friction this summer as they pop up on the island of Antiparos, in a space called Maison Bardot, a cultural center not far from the beach. Maison Bardot’s aesthetic is typically Cycladic — lime and clay surfaces, pigmented terracotta floors, diffused light — so much so that it temporarily scrambled my brain to see pieces like this blue-legged Sottsass bookcase or a laminated wood Mendini chair inside it. But I Could Never Have Anticipated What Would Make It So Great. by Jill Singer If you can believe it, this was my first year attending 3DaysofDesign in Copenhagen, and I went to the fair, now in its 10th year, armed with absurdly high expectations. I knew that just existing in Copenhagen in early June — using Lime bikes to cycle around, drinking natural wine, eating smørrebrød — would set a good baseline for fun. But after my experience at Salone, which I wrote about here , I felt increasingly desperate for Copenhagen to mean something . I told people I was going because, as a chronicler of design fair culture, I felt compelled to see one that had become such a word-of-mouth success. But on a personal level, it’s like I needed Copenhagen to prove to me that design fairs were still worth attending. As hesitant as I am to say this — lest everyone frantically start planning their show next year in Denmark, which is simply not the right move for everyone — Copenhagen actually exceeded my expectations. As I went through the week, seeing the precise things where, to me, Milan fell short — i.e. incredible group shows assembled by designers and brand presentations so intentional they bordered on religious — I began to develop a theory about what made this year in Copenhagen so great. I crystallized it in my group chat. “There was a matriarchal energy to 3Days that stood in stark contrast to Milan,” I wrote. “Women were at the helm of almost every company or exhibition I loved. Not to the exclusion of men at all. But in a way that I have never in my life felt at a design fair.” There were Rhya Johnston-Wallace and Kasia Sznajder, two ex-Frama employees who not only curated their own star exhibitions but also helped organize and promote presentations by a collection of mostly female-led brands or galleries . There were the big Danish brands, from Fredericia to Fritz Hansen, with their new female creative directors. There were exhibitions centered around traditional women’s crafts, like the quilts at Tekla and or the sewing exhibition at Vaerktoj. Photography: Marco Galloway When Paul Schärer took over the Swiss manufacturer USM in the 1960s, he commissioned the influential architectect Fritz Haller to design its new headquarters. Haller responded with a flexible, modular chromed framework that could be reconfigured with ball joints to the needs of the office. He then set his mind to furnishing it, and designed a range that could match the new buildings’ sleek and adaptable structure. What he came up with was a system of steel modules that could stack vertically, laterally and elegantly. A design classic with a clean, industrial minimalism and rich powder-coated colour, the USM modular system became a mid-century classic and a staple of functional spaces everywhere. They can recede into the architecture of a space or become luxurious features when displaying collectible objects, flowers, records. But we've never seen it used in this most recent application — as the foundation for this new bar by New York entrepreneur Josh Greenspan. Photography: Marco Galloway 1 of 4 VV's Cocktail Room, named for Greenspan's daughter, Vivienne, was inspired by late nights in New York and omakases in Tokyo . Photography: courtesy of Run For the Hills Shifting lifestyle preferences have fuelled popularity for kitchen-diners, breakfast bars and sofa suppers. But does that mean dedicated eating spaces are heading for extinction? While a report by Aviva released last month found that one in five homeowners has repurposed the dining room, it seems not everyone is clamouring to phase them out. A new generation of designers is reimagining the dining room in a convivial, flexible way that’s neither stuffy nor formal — as a place not only for a special occasion but also for a random Tuesday, as a place to quietly gather away from the chaos of the kitchen. ‘If you do a dining room right and make it a space that’s not just for family Christmases, you’ll use it far more than an old-style stuffy space,’ says Anna Burles, cofounder of interiors studio Run For the Hills . ‘Make it cosy, casually glamorous and comfortable enough to feel right for regular, old family dinners — phones and devices left at the door. But also make it the perfect spot for laying out boardgames or a jigsaw or setting up a craft project that’s not in the main kitchen. Luckily, the Shop AD team has done our fair share of moving, sometimes multiple times in a single year. And while our college cutlery and starter apartment towels have served us well over the years, it's never a bad time for a fresh start. So we asked ourselves: If we were outfitting our homes from scratch, what would we buy first? These are our starter home essentials—spanning bed , bath , and kitchen—we recommend time and time again. In every category, you’ll find three options: an entry-level pick for those just getting started, an AD -tested favorite, and a splurge-worthy option for those ready to upgrade. Whether you’re buying, renting, moving in, or moving on, consider this your guide to setting up a home with style and longevity in mind. Beatz graced the cover of AD in 2021 in the art-filled modernist home he shares with Alicia Keys. Courtesy of CB2 Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story When it comes to designing your first furniture collection with CB2, appearing on the cover of Architectural Digest and owning an iconic home—like Wallace E. Cunningham ’s Razor House —certainly give you an edge. While creating the Casa Dean by Swizz Beatz line, which launched today, Kasseem “Swizz Beatz” Dean, the Grammy-winning producer behind some of Beyoncé, Jay-Z, and Drake’s biggest records, found that music and design flex the same artistic muscles. The line explores family-friendly home design through a creative lens—with art-inspired upholstery, lighting, wall decor, rugs, and glassware that all encourage quality time with loved ones. “My goal for the collection was to bring families together, which is why I named it after my family,” says Dean. “I wanted to design what I thought was the creative home for all creatives—no matter what medium you choose.” The bubble-stemmed glasses are another standout to the producer and artist. “I imagined these pieces as sculptures, so whether you’re using or viewing them, they always feel like art.” Courtesy of CB2 The Brainstorm Leather Accent Chair upholstered in Dean’s favorite shade of British Racing Green. Courtesy of CB2 Developed with Evan Jerry, founder of Studio ANANSI and a member of CB2’s Designer Collective, the line is saturated in earth tones, curved edges, and luxurious textures. Billal Taright Design + Decorate House Tours This Art Collector’s Southampton Home Plays by Its Own Rules This Art Collector’s Southampton Home Plays by Its Own Rules With an expanding gallery, his first furniture line, and a growing portfolio of interiors, ascending designer Patrick McGrath shows off his mix-master flair. By Sarah Cristobal Published: Oct 11, 2026 Save Article Share Article 4 min read Above: In the primary bedroom of a Southampton, NY, house updated by designer Patrick McGrath, a Robert Longo drawing overlooks circa 1930 R.C. Coquery lounge chairs and a Marcel Breuer table. Vitsoe shelves host an Andy Warhol Brillo Box and a Jordan McDonald vase. So me say the world will end in fire/Some say in ice. Those opening lines to Robert Frost’s apocalyptic 1920 poem “Fire and Ice” provided unlikely inspiration for a line of candles created by interior designer Patrick McGrath that will debut this holiday season. Such a foreboding, intense reference point might seem to belie the confident affability that has endeared McGrath to a range of clients, whether New York City hedge-funders, Hong Kong antiquities collectors, or friends turned collaborators. The latter include fashion designer Francisco Costa, whose brand, Costa Brazil, partnered with McGrath on the new candles. “Patrick has great vision and direction,” Costa says. “He’s great at interpreting style—old and new—and bringing it together effortlessly.” Billal Taright McGrath furnished the dining room with a Pierre Chapo table and chairs from the 1960s and installed a Ruemmler pendant light above. The sideboard is Charles Dudouyt from the 1940s; Farrow & Ball paint; sisal rug by Crosby Street Studios. For one of his latest projects, McGrath injected a heavy dose of sophisticated style into a house on Long Island’s East End for a thirtysomething bachelor and art collector whose Soho apartment he had designed years earlier. Located in the desirable Estate Section of Southampton, the 1970s shingle home featured interiors that were, as the designer puts it, “classic Hamptons floral.” Not exactly compatible with the new owner’s collection of contemporary works by artists such as Rashid Johnson, Vik Muniz, and Nate Lowman. items.text: The Webster opens first hotel in London - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search The Webster opens first hotel in London 9 October 2026 • Projects The Webster Covent Garden has opened its doors, marking the debut of the new design-forward lifestyle hotel brand in London. Set overlooking Lincoln’s Inn Fields, the 167-bedroom hotel brings together thoughtful design, literary inspiration, distinctive food and drink and a programme of culture and connection. Designed by London-based architecture and interior design studio Red Deer, The Webster Covent Garden draws on the idea of magical realism, the literary genre famously associated with Colombian writer Gabriel García Márquez – taking a grounded, real setting and introducing subtle moments of wonder. This spirit runs throughout the hotel, where warmth, texture and storytelling transforms overlooked corners into spaces that invite curiosity and intrigue. The design unfolds gradually, with expressive details bringing together contemporary sophistication and a sense of nostalgia. Bespoke furniture sits alongside expressive materials and artwork by British artists including Henry Ward and Emily Kirby, while Italian-terrazzo-inspired flooring adds a graphic rhythm throughout the space. Intimate library nooks offer quieter moments to read, work or linger within the hotel’s more social settings, and – at the heart of it all – the outdoor lounge and terrace take on a different character throughout the day. The hotel features 167 guestrooms, including three suites across 10 floors, each conceived as a serene, character-rich sanctuary with a timeless sensibility. Warm neutral palettes of terracotta, oxblood and soft off-whites, inspired by historic interiors, literary salons and old publishing houses, are paired with textured plank flooring, hand-knotted wool rugs and bespoke brass and alabaster lighting. Carefully selected objects bring a sense of nostalgia to the rooms, from Robert Radios and hand-selected books, inviting guests to disconnect from the digital world. A mid-century-style elbow chair adds to the timeless character, while bespoke artwork and custom-patterned drapery bring moments of wonder. Throughout, the design balances comfort and sophistication with playful details and unexpected charm. Bathrooms continue the calm, considered aesthetic, with terrazzo flooring and organic ceramic wall tiles in neutral tones, complemented by brushed-nickel Kohler fixtures and softly illuminated mirrors. At the centre of the hotel’s social offering is a trio of food and beverage destinations. On the lower ground floor, Carmelina’s is the hotel’s signature Italian-inspired restaurant, featuring a nostalgic black-and-white tiled floor, warm natural materials and classic Italian-inspired interiors. items.text: The Shepherd Mayfair opens its doors - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search The Shepherd Mayfair opens its doors 8 October 2026 • Projects The Shepherd Mayfair has officially opened in Shepherd Market, introducing an 82-room boutique hotel shaped by the history and social character of one of London’s most distinctive neighbourhoods. Designed by Timothy Shepherd of Shepherd&, the new hotel brings together individually configured rooms and suites, a collection of British art and tailored wellness and lifestyle partnerships. Dining destinations Fayre and The Lounge have also opened, while Teddy’s, the hotel’s late-night cocktail bar, will follow in November 2026. The Shepherd Mayfair stands on the site of Mayfair’s oldest house, known as The Cottage, which dates to 1618 and was once home to a shepherd tending his flock. The surrounding fields later hosted the annual May Fair before architect and developer Edward Shepherd transformed the area into the intimate quarter that still bears his name. The Shepherd Mayfair draws this history into a contemporary interpretation of Mayfair’s historic mansions, pairing the refinement of a private residence with the independent spirit of the area. The Shepherd Mayfair is a joint venture between Bain Capital and Orka Investments. Spanning 33,600ft 2 across six floors, the hotel features references to local figures including Desmond Sautter, Lord Sandwich and Tiddy Doll, alongside Braille and Morse details that recall the area’s wartime intelligence history and nearby Down Street station. The Shepherd Mayfair has 70 rooms and 12 suites, each configured around the proportions of the original mansion layouts. Categories range from Standard and Superior Rooms to the larger Shepherd Suites and Mayfair Suites, with many rooms incorporating window seats overlooking Shepherd Market and Mayfair. Adaptable furniture responds to the practical needs of travellers: desks convert into dressing tables, console tables become chessboards and integrated storage keeps rooms calm and uncluttered. Marble bathrooms feature bespoke Floris London amenities, with selected rooms offering bathtubs and separate seating areas. On the ground floor, Fayre is a 62-cover neighbourhood restaurant serving breakfast, lunch and dinner. Its banquettes, dark timber panelling and berry-toned palette are set beneath wall coverings by British artist Adam Ellis, whose scenes reinterpret the traders, performers and spectacle of the original May Fair. A three-metre chandelier developed by Shepherd& with Somerset-based Cantelo Lighting brings together more than 500 individually suspended amber glass pendants in a brushed brass structure. At street level, The Lounge is a 46-cover all-day café and bar with an outdoor terrace and a street-facing hatch for takeaway refreshments. items.text: Wimberly Interiors refreshes JW Marriott suite with New York-inspired scheme - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search Wimberly Interiors refreshes JW Marriott suite with New York-inspired scheme 6 October 2026 • Projects Wimberly Interiors has completed the redesign of JW Marriott Essex House’s Promenade Suite. Situated on the 38th floor, the suite is envisioned as a singular expression of luxury within the hotel’s iconic Art Deco tower. Inspired by The Promenade, also known as The Mall and Literary Walk in Central Park, and New York City’s cultural character, the design creates a dialogue between the interiors and the city beyond. Expansive windows frame unobstructed views of Central Park, the East River and the Hudson River, making the panorama an integral part of the experience and linking the interiors to the park’s landscape and the New York skyline. “Luxury today is about creating spaces that feel personal, memorable, and connected to their surroundings,” says Liana Hawes Young, Associate Principal, Wimberly Interiors. “For the Promenade Suite, we looked to Central Park, the hotel’s Art Deco heritage, and New York’s cultural institutions to inform every layer of the design, from the material palette to the artwork and furnishings.” Organised around an expansive parlour, open kitchen and dining area, the 1,390ft 2 suite provides a natural setting for gathering. Two bedrooms extend directly from these central living spaces. Through adjoining connections, either a king guestroom or a one-bedroom suite can be added, allowing the accommodation to expand to a three- or four-bedroom configuration on the 38 th floor. The planning strategy balances flexibility with residential scale and privacy. The design team introduced subtle references to nearby Lincoln Center and the Metropolitan Opera through a palette of rich merlot, aubergine and green balanced by softer hues inspired by Central Park. Warm woods, burnished metals, geometric detailing and richly textured wallcoverings acknowledge Art Deco influences. Tailored furnishings and select vintage pieces bring a curated residential quality. Classic motifs and natural stones appear in unexpected applications that allow familiar elements to feel current within the space. Artwork curated by Ryan Art Advisory, including pieces by New York-based artist Scott VanderVoort and Brooklyn-based artist Tess Michalik, complements the material palette through abstract geometry and botanical compositions, celebrating craftsmanship and New York’s contemporary creative community. Materiality and colour selections carry through the central living spaces into every bedroom within the configuration to support a cohesive aesthetic while giving each room its own identity. The two bedrooms connected directly to the main suite are colour drenched, one in merlot and the other in green, with both walls and ceilings fully enveloped. items.text: Ruby makes French debut with hotel and workspaces - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search Ruby makes French debut with hotel and workspaces 5 October 2026 • Projects Ruby , an urban lifestyle hotel and part of IHG Hotels & Resorts, opens Ruby Lilou in Marseille, marking the brand’s debut in France. Inspired by Marseille’s distinctive blend of Mediterranean ease and rebellious creativity, Ruby Lilou reflects the brand’s signature approach to creating hotels deeply connected to their destination. Set between the historic Vieux Port and the creative energy of La Joliette, the new hotel pairs thoughtful design with laid-back social spaces, a sun-drenched rooftop terrace and a warm, easy-going spirit. Ruby Lilou’s design draws directly from its locale, with soft tones drawn from lavender fields, sun-bleached stone and the Mediterranean Sea, layered with graphic patterns, bold colours and unexpected references to the city’s rebellious creative culture. The hotel features 237 rooms across the Nest, Cosy, Lovely and Wow categories, combining intelligent use of space with premium comfort. Inspired by luxury yacht design, every room offers oversized beds, walk-in rainfall showers, blackout curtains and carefully curated interiors that reflect Marseille’s maritime heritage and creative spirit. Ruby Lilou also reflects the brand’s focus on soulful, city-centre stays for cosmopolitan, lifestyle-focused travellers, combining central locations, distinctive design and seamless, tech-enabled experiences. Music is woven throughout the experience, from curated sound programmes to live acts in the evening and in-room Marshall amplifiers and Bluetooth speakers. At the heart of the hotel is Ruby’s signature 24/7 bar and café, a relaxed setting that serves beverages and light bites throughout the day. The hotel also boasts a 300m 2 rooftop terrace, which offers panoramic views across Marseille towards the Mediterranean and providing a vibrant space to relax from morning until late into the evening. Opening alongside Ruby Lilou, Ruby Yani introduces Ruby Workspaces to France for the first time. Operated by The Ruby Group, the new workspace concept offers more than 126 flexible workstations, private offices, meeting rooms, phone booths and thoughtfully designed communal areas, creating an inspiring environment for freelancers, entrepreneurs, businesses and hotel guests alike. items.text: The Hoxton to open second German outpost - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search The Hoxton to open second German outpost 2 October 2026 • Projects The Hoxton has announced that it will open a hotel in Hamburg in summer 2027, marking the brand’s second hotel in Germany and third in the German-speaking region, following Berlin and Vienna. Set in a 1950s building on Alter Wall, The Hoxton, Hamburg will feature interiors by Swedish studio Stylt Trampoli , bringing the energy of the city into its ten floors and 188 guestrooms. The hotel will also be home to a Mediterranean-inspired restaurant on the ground floor, a rooftop seafood restaurant overlooking the Elbphilharmonie, Michel and Town Hall, a private dining room for up to 20 guests and an all-day lobby bar. The Apartment, The Hoxton’s signature events space, will also feature, comprising three meeting rooms, its own pantry kitchen and a private terrace overlooking the canal. In the heart of the Nikolaiviertel, The Hoxton will be surrounded by a mix of old and new, with historic buildings sitting alongside modern architecture, independent shops, galleries and cultural spots. The interiors take their cues from Alter Wall and the surrounding neighbourhood, with the history of the area woven into the hotel’s public spaces. The 188 guestrooms will be spread across six categories, including Cosy, Roomy and Biggy, and will sit between the first and eighth floors. There will also be 32 interconnecting rooms, ideal for families and friends travelling together. On the ground floor, the welcoming lobby is designed to be a homey hangout for locals and guests alike with a mix of vintage and bespoke furniture, cosy corners and artwork by local artists. “We’re incredibly excited to bring The Hoxton to Hamburg, a city known for its maritime character, thriving creative scene and vibrant cultural landscape,” says Cédric Gobilliard, COO Ennismore Europe. “The city’s mix of historic charm and contemporary energy, from its canals and neo-gothic landmarks to its thriving nightlife scene and groundbreaking modern architecture, makes it a natural fit for The Hoxton. We’re thrilled to become part of the neighbourhood and bring the brand’s distinctive take on open-house hospitality to the Nikolaiviertel.” Erik Florvaag, CEO and Managing Partner of The Chocolate on the Pillow Group, adds: “With The Hoxton, we’re bringing one of Europe’s most exciting lifestyle brands to Hamburg, a particularly attractive market for the hospitality industry in Germany. NIGHTSWIMMING – Giovanna Silva I started photographing discotheques when Monditalia commissioned a project from me on the architecture of Italian nightlife for the 2014 Venice Architecture Biennale . I must admit this was a completely unknown subject to me, which I am just beginning to get familiar with now, when the exhibition in Venice has closed and our project has become a book. My unfamiliarity with the topic surely gave me an unconventional and detached eye, but required an extra effort and the restraint of all my compulsiveness. We started by collecting the books already published on the subject: on the one hand, we needed to gather all the possible information, on the other, discotheques are buildings that change their appearance rather frequently – having to adjust to fashion, to the music, and to the progress in lighting and sound technology – therefore books were the main way of seeing images of most of the discotheques we were finding out about. These books brought actual people into the project: critics, architects, DJs, art directors, club owners… the night swimmers. items.text: Transforming Barcelona's Waterfront: A Story of Urban Renewal | ArchDaily ArchDaily Articles Transforming Barcelona's Waterfront: A Story of Urban Renewal Transforming Barcelona's Waterfront: A Story of Urban Renewal Listen to this article 6:11 Listen to this article 6:11 Playing this article Port of Barcelona in the foreground and Montserrat Mountain at top left. . Image © M McBey via Wikipedia under license CC BY 2.0 Written by Moises Carrasco Published on October 16, 2026 As one walks along the beachfront of Barcelona , the shoreline feels like it has always been there: sand, palm trees, a long promenade, restaurants, shops and modern hotels, when the reality is that it has not always been this way. Until the 1980s, Barcelona 's seafront was a working barrier of railway lines, factories and informal housing, and wastewater ran straight into the Mediterranean. Starting in 1987, Barcelona has continuously created large promenades and passages between the city and the sea, creating an environment that today many might read as previously empty space, but is actually the result of decades of infrastructure and social complexity, along with a municipal effort to transform the city's territory and its relationship to the water. Following that transformation raises three questions that frame this article: who was displaced to open the waterfront, who governs it today, and who keeps it standing? + 2 The first attempt to create a relationship with the water dates back to the late 1980s, in preparation for the 1992 Olympics, according to a 2025 review on the topic by N. Benach and N. Font-Casaseca. For decades prior, a railway line had separated Barcelona's industrial fabric from the sea, and shanty towns existed along the city's coastline, on beaches like Somorrostro. The same review places the concrete start of these efforts in 1987, with the Spatial Plan of Port Vell and the Moll de la Fusta. According to J. Henrich i Monrás , this plan grew out of a broader urban study published by the City of Barcelona, Àrees de Nova Centralitat , and aimed to replace port and storage functions with leisure, hotels and commercial uses. Paseo Maritimo in Barcelona. Image © Moises Carrasco The Olympic works then gave that vision its physical form. Benach and Font-Casaseca also describe how the rail line was buried and how wastewater, previously discharged directly into the Mediterranean, began to be treated. At the same time, the city created and stabilised new beaches, improved access along the coast, and delivered the Vila Olímpica and a marina on former industrial land in Poblenou. Yet they also point out that the waterfront was never empty to begin with. It was full of industrial sites, housing and, as mentioned, shanty towns. In that light, they note that opening the city to the sea meant clearing an area that, by the mid-twentieth century, hosted around 15,000 people. Surrounded by thirty-six hectares of protected jungle linking two nature reserves, over ninety percent of the land remains entirely untouched. Low impact updates will be made to La Valise Bacalar to elevate the guest experience while honouring its regenerative spirit. Light-touch changes to the wellness areas, rooftop, cenote-style pool and lagoon deck will come later this year. Image credit: La Valise Bacalar The hotel’s architecture was masterminded by celebrated Mexican architect Frida Escobedo , known to design enthusiasts as the youngest architect to design London’s Serpentine Pavilion in 2018. At La Valise Bacalar, Escobedo’s design philosophy ensures that nothing is imposed on the land, with timber treehouse suites and villas which rise lightly on stilts above the forest floor, protecting the underlying soil and surrounding root systems. Under Namron Hospitality, the property will enter its next chapter as La Valise Bacalar, joining La Valise hotels in Mexico City, Tulum, San Miguel de Allende, Mazunte and Los Cabos. The expansion builds on a brand that began with founder and CEO Yves Naman’s transformation of a 1920s townhouse in Mexico City into the original La Valise, establishing an approach to hospitality centered on intimate scale, individual design and a strong connection to place. The upcoming Hamburg debut marks the next step in the brand’s European growth, with openings also planned in Oslo and Madrid next year . Set in a 1950s building on Alter Wall, The Hoxton, Hamburg will bring the energy of the city into its ten floors and 188 rooms. Alongside the bedrooms, there’ll be a Mediterranean-inspired restaurant on the ground floor, a rooftop seafood restaurant overlooking the Elbphilharmonie, Michel and Town Hall, a private dining room for up to 20 guests and an all-day lobby bar. Image credit: Ennismore The hotel will also be home to The Apartment, The Hoxton’s signature events space, with three meeting rooms, its own pantry kitchen and a private terrace overlooking the canal. In the heart of the Nikolaiviertel, the property will be surrounded by a mix of old and new, with historic buildings sitting alongside modern architecture, independent shops, galleries and cultural spots. The interiors, designed by Swedish studio Stylt Trampoli , take their cues from Alter Wall and the surrounding neighbourhood, with the history of the area woven into the hotel’s public spaces. The 188 rooms will be spread across six categories, including ‘Cosy’, ‘Roomy’ and ‘Biggy’, and will sit between the first and eighth floors. There will also be 32 interconnecting rooms, ideal for families and friends travelling together. Image credit: Ennismore On the ground floor, the welcoming lobby is designed to be a homey hangout for locals and guests alike with a mix of vintage and bespoke furniture, cosy corners and artwork by local artists, alongside the vibrant all-day bar. items.text: Pelican House - anchoring the bedroom moodboard • Hotel Designs Subscribe News Resource Hub Hotel Suppliers Hotel Industry Network Supplier News On The Boards Hotel Reviews Spotlight On In Conversation Hotel Designs LABS SPACE Magazine DESIGN POD Guide To Hotel Design Editor’s Picks Events Industry Events MEET UP London MEET UP North The Brit List Awards Accessible Design Talks Hotel Summit Interior Design & Architecture Summit Newsletter Contact Us SUBSCRIBE Hotel Designs Hotel Designs News Hotel Suppliers On The Boards SPACE Magazine Events Industry Events MEET UP London MEET UP North The Brit List Awards Accessible Design Talks Hotel Summit Interior Design & Architecture Summit Pelican House – anchoring the bedroom moodboard WORDS BY Pauline Brettell October 14, 2026 Sanderson ADA Grohe Atkinson Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Pelican House – anchoring the bedroom moodboard A hotel bedroom has to feel like somewhere the person sleeping in it belongs. It has to feel considered down to the smallest decision, and still feel effortless: a sanctuary that puts you fully at ease while staying connected to the place around it… A rug has a large part to play i n that role. It either sits back and quietly completes a room through colour, material and texture, or it steps forward and ties the whole thing together through layered, storytelling design. Which way a room needs it, depends on everything happening above the rug, the busier the headboard or palette, the more that choice matters. A bedroom rug also takes more barefoot traffic than any other rug in the building, and sits close enough to the bed that its scale has to answer to the bed. It has to feel considered underfoot for the two-hundredth guest. Image credit: The Hoxton Image credit: Kin House / Barlow & Barlow At The Hoxton, Dublin, a bordered Pelican House rug in olive and oxblood plays it bold, matching a busy checkerboard headboard pattern for pattern and tying the room together by meeting its energy head on. At Kin House, Barlow & Barlow made the same bold call from the floor up, a red-and-cream checkerboard running to the edge of a canopy bed, anchoring the room rather than sitting beneath it quietly. In Emma Ainscough’s Chelsea bedroom, the opposite move: a pale rug scattered with tiny florals sits beneath a deep green headboard, understated enough you’d only notice it by its absence. And at Casa Coco in Oaxaca, Mexico, that same restraint moves onto the wall, where hand-braided woven art from Pelican House hangs above the beds. Bold or subtle, what makes either possible is the same: a handmade piece brings age-old craftsmanship and cultural layering into a space that no machine-made equivalent can fake. Image credit: Emma Ainscough At Pelican House, it’s not just about how a rug is made, but who made it. Created and owned by two Icelandic families, the 31-room hotel combines individually designed rooms and suites with geothermal wellness, seasonal cuisine and wide views across the surrounding countryside. Here, the changing weather, vast skies and open landscape are part of the experience. Image credit: 360 Hotel Iceland The hotel’s location is one of its greatest advantages. Just one hour from Reykjavík and 15 minutes from Selfoss, it provides an ideal base for exploring some of Iceland’s most celebrated landscapes and attractions, from the Golden Circle and South Coast to Vík, with longer journeys possible towards Jökulsárlón. Guests can make day trips in different directions and return to the same welcoming base each evening rather than packing up and moving on. It is a way to see more of Iceland while travelling at a slower pace, with time to enjoy the hotel, the landscape and the experience in between. The South Iceland experience begins at the hotel itself. The extraordinary Icelandic light and uninterrupted views across the countryside are part of everyday life here, and an afternoon by the fire can be just as much a part of experiencing Iceland as a day spent exploring the landscape. items.text: Case study: Lutron – lighting the next chapter of a legendary London hotel • Hotel Designs Subscribe News Resource Hub Hotel Suppliers Hotel Industry Network Supplier News On The Boards Hotel Reviews Spotlight On In Conversation Hotel Designs LABS SPACE Magazine DESIGN POD Guide To Hotel Design Editor’s Picks Events Industry Events MEET UP London MEET UP North The Brit List Awards Accessible Design Talks Hotel Summit Interior Design & Architecture Summit Newsletter Contact Us SUBSCRIBE Hotel Designs Hotel Designs News Hotel Suppliers On The Boards SPACE Magazine Events Industry Events MEET UP London MEET UP North The Brit List Awards Accessible Design Talks Hotel Summit Interior Design & Architecture Summit Case study: Lutron – lighting the next chapter of a legendary London hotel WORDS BY Pauline Brettell October 13, 2026 Sanderson ADA Grohe Atkinson Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Case study: Lutron – lighting the next chapter of a legendary London hotel For more than 135 years, The Savoy has stood as a defining presence on the banks of the Thames. Since its debut in 1889, the iconic hotel has set the standard for luxury hospitality. Here, elegance is a way of life and history, and modernity are woven seamlessly together… The roll call of those who have passed through its revolving doors reads like a who’s who. Claude Monet captured the shimmering Thames from his suite window. A young Guccio Gucci, then a luggage porter, internalised the hotel’s impeccable standards before channelling them into one of fashion’s most iconic empires. From Hollywood royalty to actual royalty, artists to iconoclasts, the Savoy has always attracted a discerning clientele. From the very beginning, the hotel manifested a talent for the revolutionary. London’s first luxury hotel rewrote the rulebook by introducing electric lighting, lifts, and en-suite bathrooms at a time when such comforts bordered on science fiction. That instinct for innovation, for being quietly, confidently ahead of the curve, has never left the building. Architecturally, The Savoy tells its story in two distinct chapters. The Edwardian rooms, many gazing out across the Thames, speak in the language of classical grandeur and the hushed tones of cultural refinement. Along the Strand, the Art Deco interiors make their entrance with bold geometry, theatrical glamour, a space that demands a cocktail and a story. Two eras, one enduring address. Image credit: GA / What the Fox Studios Embracing duality It is precisely this duality between the familiar and the fearlessly new, that sets the tone for the latest guest room refurbishment, completed in 2026. Behind this renovation stands a collective of extraordinary talent including co-owner, Kingdom Hotel Investments; client representatives, Artizan Group; GA, responsible for the interior and architectural design; Nulty, lighting design consultants; and Accor, the multinational hospitality group, to name just a few. The property will comprise 285 fully equipped studios, each with a private kitchen, alongside co-working space, a lobby lounge, luggage storage, shared kitchen, laundry facilities, a tech-powered guest shop and car and bicycle parking. Image credit: Bob W The signing comes as Bob W scales across both established and new European markets . The company currently operates in 12 countries, with its contracted footprint set to reach at least 18 by the end of 2028. Alongside continued growth across the UK, Nordics and DACH, Bob W is expanding across Southern Europe, including Spain, Italy and Portugal, while also targeting opportunities in Benelux and Eastern Europe. Alexanderplatz reflects a parallel shift in the scale of opportunities the company is pursuing. Bob W’s model gives it the flexibility to operate both smaller and larger properties, with larger properties already operating across multiple markets. As its real estate proposition has matured, Bob W is increasingly targeting larger assets of 150 keys and above, with Alexanderplatz providing its clearest example to date. Located in Berlin-Mitte, approximately 100 metres from Alexanderplatz station, the property sits close to major landmarks including the Berlin TV Tower, Museum Island, Berlin Cathedral and Hackescher Markt. It also benefits from extensive S-Bahn, U-Bahn, regional rail, tram and bus connections. The deal builds on an existing relationship between Bob W and Aroundtown, who also collaborated on the conversion of Dortmund’s former main post office at Königswall 1-3.
