Christian Rodriguez Nadia Chaudhury is a born-and-raised New Yorker who is the deputy editor for Eater’s Northeast region and Eater New York, was the former Eater Austin editor for 10 years, and often writes about food and pop culture. The bad news: Vibrant tasting menu restaurant HAGS is closing in the East Village. The good news: Co-owners chef Telly Justice and sommelier Camille Lindsley are in the middle of relocating their queer restaurant to Noho next year. The original East Village location, at 163 First Avenue near East 10th Street, is having its final day on Sunday, October 18, with a last pay-what-you-can brunch from 11 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. And then, HAGS 2.0 will open in Noho at 334 Bowery and East Third Street in January or February 2027. Justice tells Eater that the team signed the Bowery lease in June and began working on the new space at the beginning of September. They told their First Avenue landlord about leaving the address, using their good guy clause (which allows them to get out of a commercial real estate lease with fair notice). It turns out that “a very energized, enthusiastic tenant,” per Justice, wanted to take over the address as soon as possible, which meant they had to leave in 30 days. HAGS tried to extend their lease, but they couldn’t make it work. “We can’t fault them for that; they’re doing their job, we’re doing ours,” Justice says. The staff is getting what she describes as a “lengthy severance,” adding that “everybody’s going to get a nice long paid vacation, myself included, and I think we all need and deserve that right now.” (HAGS’s name works two-fold : it stands for “Have a Good Summer” and references the word that Merriam-Webster describes as an “evil-looking old woman.”) The Noho restaurant is larger than the 20-seat East Village location, with about 60 to 70 seats. Nadia Chaudhury Nadia Chaudhury is a born-and-raised New Yorker who is the deputy editor for Eater’s Northeast region and Eater New York, was the former Eater Austin editor for 10 years, and often writes about food and pop culture. In our Dining Reports, we share a firsthand perspective of a recent restaurant visit, covering everything from the vibe to must-get dishes. See more in the Eater app. Download the app After competing and becoming a finalist in the 23rd season of Top Chef in the Carolinas, Sherry Cardoso (who had been an opening chef at Olmsted, among other positions) came back to New York to debut her tasting menu at Cynthia , her West Village restaurant, with co-founder and business partner Claire DuBois. It’s named after DuBois’s aunt, Cynthia Peck, who had co-run Fullerton, California restaurants Angelo’s and Vinci’s Ristorante. The $165 six-course menu reflects Cardoso: New American dishes with plenty of Brazilian aspects — and an eye on sustainability, using ends, peels, and trimmings. (There’s a seven-course option for $200.) Each meal is preceded by a cute card describing the seasonal significance and produce in poetic language. The space is a single airy dining room, with a soundtrack heavy on the 1990s, comfortable seats, and a bathroom sink seemingly carved out of a huge rock . What you’ll get I went during the summer. The presentation of the fluke tostada in the opening bites section was so neat and unexpected. Cardoso tops a yellow masa tostada with fluke lightly layered in a creamy, nutty vatapa sauce, laced with shrimp and coconut, then garnished with a sheet of nori. The corn course featuring lots of squash was such a wonderfully complex grouping, with corn served three ways: First, there’s a corn sorbet with tiny sliced squash; the two-layer creamy corn custard topped with caviar; then the roasted summer squash with corn kernels and dollops of a chunky XO sauce made with vegetable trim, lending to a beautiful pairing of sweet and savory tastes

The flagship is the namesake 150-seat Japanese fine-dining restaurant led by chefs Tadaaki Ishizaki and Shuji Furukawa, offering both a la carte and a tasting menu that threads French techniques by way of Japanese ingredients. Ishizaki had been the culinary director for two-Michelin-starred Odo; Furukawa led the Michelin-starred Restaurant Yuu. Two counters tuck into the space beyond the flagship: One is Kumiko Room , a 14-seat omakase sushi bar from master Edomae sushi chef Yoshihiko Kousaka , whose restaurants (Jewel Bako, Kosaka) have also landed Michelin stars. Both are opening on Thursday, October 15. The drink list will include more than 500 sake and French wine selections, Japanese whisky, and refined cocktails. The third space involves the relocation of Kappo Sono , a 10-seat kaiseki experience led by chef Chikara Sono (formerly of Michelin-starred Kyo Ya). Gjelina has been a restaurant people fawn over, particularly when it first opened in 2008, serving pristine vegetables and admirable breads in LA’s Venice. She mentions Schrager’s support and designer Dominic Kozerski , in addition to the kitchen staff, as what make the project exciting. Facebook Link Thomas Straker, the London-based celebrity chef with more than two million followers on both Instagram and TikTok, is known for viral cooking videos, a cookbook, and an almost-evangelical enthusiasm for butter . Now he’s bringing his cooking to Straker’s, at 59 Grand Street, at West Broadway, in Soho, taking over the former Lucky Strike space, with the restaurant officially opening Saturday, October 10. The New York opening lands alongside a major U.S. expansion for Straker’s butter business: His British butter is now sold in Whole Foods stores around the country. Ahead of the opening, I spoke with Straker about why he chose New York, what he’s bringing over from London, and the year-delayed, roughly $2 million-over-budget transformation of Lucky Strike. This interview, which first appeared on Eater New York Substack, has been edited and condensed for clarity. Why New York? Thomas Straker: The dining scene here is completely different. People live outside of their apartments in New York — they’re out having breakfast, lunch, dinner — whereas in London there’s a lot more eating at home. People might eat out twice a week there; here, you end up eating out all the time. The market is so strong. If you do something that has an appeal, you can almost guarantee you’re going to be busy. And I have a U.S. passport. I was born in Washington, D.C., so I thought, I’m either going to use it or lose it. I wanted to explore how to build the brand abroad. I didn’t want to open more of the same restaurants in London, and I didn’t really fancy any other cities in the U.K. So I thought, why not? I’m American. Claudia Martel How will the New York menu differ from London? Straker: The menu structure is going to remain pretty much the same, almost unchanged. Facebook Link Chef Nancy Silverton debuted her Pacific Palisades restaurant Spacca Tutto on Thursday, October 15, as an opening the enclave needs. After the Palisades Fire tore through the coastal community in January 2025 , the neighborhood lost homes, residents, and nearly a dozen restaurants , along with damage to its centerpiece Palisades Village. Palisades Village owner Rick Caruso recently reopened his retail and restaurant property, where Silverton will debut a menu inspired by sister restaurant Chi Spacca in Hollywood, a modern Italian steakhouse. As you travel on the Palisades–Malibu–Santa Monica stretch of Pacific Coast Highway, you can still see extensive impacts from the Palisades Fire. Entire properties sit ravaged and empty, some with tattered blue tarps and wild brush overgrowth, while others are peppered with construction crews deep in the rebuilding process. Many of Pacific Palisades’ wildfire survivors remain scattered throughout the Southland. But now they can return to Palisades Village, which is still under construction. Some restaurants have opened in recent months, including Porta Via , Alphabet Bar and Grill , and, as of Thursday, Spacca Tutto. Caruso, a major fan of Chi Spacca, invited Silverton to create Spacca Tutto’s menu. “The first person I thought of was Nancy,” Caruso told Eater in 2025. “She’s an L.A. original. So I cold-called her and said, ‘I’ve got a big, crazy idea.’” Nancy Silverton. Anne Fishbein Once on board, Silverton got busy building the menu. Jeremy Fox’s beloved Santa Monica restaurant, Birdie G’s , will resurrect at Fairmont Century Plaza after closing at the end of 2025. Named after Fox’s daughter Birdie and grandmother Gladys, the restaurant will reopen on October 26, serving breakfast, lunch, and dinner with a mix of original favorites, such as the Pickle Chick, and new dishes, including a Rancho Gordo bean–based poached egg ribollita. When Fox first spoke with Fairmont Century Plaza about Birdie’s G’s in June 2025, it was supposed to be the restaurant’s second location. But as it became increasingly clear that the Bergamot Station Arts Center outpost could not remain open, nothing was set in stone; at the time of the closure, Fox believed Birdie G’s might be gone for good. “In life, you very rarely get second chances, and in a restaurant even less so,” he says. “So I feel very fortunate and grateful that I didn’t have to tell Birdie that her restaurant was done.” Jeremy Fox at Birdie G’s. Birdie G’s Chicken and vegetables. Legendary Los Angeles diner Swingers opens in the former Silver Lake All Day Baby space on Tuesday, October 20. Smash burger restaurant Heavy Handed previously occupied the storefront, opening on the corner in March 2025 before closing just a year later in spring 2026. Swingers will initially open with takeout only, with the dining room slated to open fully in December. Swingers first opened on Beverly Boulevard in 1993 , slinging steaming cups of coffee and French toast until the early hours of the morning. The iconic Googie cafe inspired the 1996 movie Swingers (although the film was shot at the former 101 Coffee Shop) and appeared in other Hollywood productions, including Knocked Up and Insecure. The diner has long held a special place in Angelenos’ hearts, conjuring memories of late-night breakfasts in plaid booths with dishes splayed across gleaming orange tables. Swinger’s announced it would close permanently in April 2020 due to impacts of the pandemic , but reopened in November 2020 under new owner Stephanie Wilson , the former general manager who has been with the restaurant since 2010 in different roles. Wilson tells Eater she long believed Swingers would do well in the Silver Lake area and had been looking for the right home; when the former All Day Baby space became available, it just felt right, she says. Marée strives to be more casual (the final bill may beg to differ, however), with an approachable wine list — no cocktails here — and polished French dishes like mussels “gratin,” grilled Caledonian prawn cocktail, and grilled pork chop dressed in herbaceous Cafe de Paris sauce. The fairly spartan room, which used to be beloved Peruvian restaurant Picca and then the fancy Michelin-starred Manzke, has soaring ceilings that contribute to an increasingly rowdy scene as the evening progresses. Warmth comes from the weathered hand-drawn menus on the wall mirrors, as well as the open kitchen that churns out grilled hamburgers au poivre — about 25 per night, to create just the right amount of fervor around them. Marée may be the freshest bistro in Los Angeles, but it already feels lived in. What to order Cute, creamy mussels au “gratin” are the ideal starter, slurped up like warm oysters and amplified by a basket of plush baguette slices, anchovies, baby radishes, and softened butter. A proper bistro meal needs some bite-building interaction to get you in the mood. Grilled Caledonian shrimp “cocktail” comes with an adorable metal bird lemon squeezer to dab on acid to every bite. Facebook Link Matilda’s , a new powerhouse bakery that mostly sells more than 3,000 pastries every week, opened in early October in a restored 1940s administrative building at the Santa Monica Airport. With so much early interest, the bakery has already experienced 45-minute lines with customers clamoring to secure croissants, sausage rolls, Danishes, cookies, sandwiches, baguettes, and sample Matilda’s butter tasting menu, which encompasses eight different tastes and styles. Owner and restaurateur Sean Martin took over the building in 2022 and recruited former social marketing campaign maker and founding baker Francois Pied. Pied tells Eater he’s been overwhelmed by the response. “I am still processing it, to be honest,” he says. “I was not expecting this level of commitment from people to stand in line.” On October 12, the shop issued an Instagram apology and thanked those who stood in line for pastries its first few weeks. Pied, who was born in France, tapped Abel Pulsifer (Brooklyn’s Radio Bakery ) as lead baker; the duo met at Bub and Grandma’s before working on Matilda’s, which is named after Martin’s daughter. Matilda starts by sourcing its flour from Hayden Flour Mills, which specializes in reviving ancient and forgotten grains. The duo slow-ferments their pastry dough for at least 18 hours, with a four-day process for butter, ham and cheese, almond, or pain au chocolat croissants. The menu also offers chocolate chip cookies, sausage rolls that have been flying off the shelves, and honey butter or traditional brioche. In Austin, which went without a major pro sports team until Austin FC’s inaugural season in 2021, college football reigns supreme. Nothing beats the roar of 100,00 at Darrell K Royal Memorial Stadium, but you can’t watch the Longhorns in person every day. For those other, non-Longhorn days, there are tons of bars in town with football, basketball, soccer, baseball, and hockey dominating screens all year long. No matter what team you’re rooting for, these sports bars have enough TVs and snacks to keep you satiated. Sausages and pitchers of beer near the University of Texas at Scholz Garten are hard to beat for ‘Horns games. If you’re a Green Bay Packers fan, there’s no place better than burger bar Billy’s on Burnet to wear your cheesehead. Soccer fans are in luck with games at Irish pub B.D. Riley’s in Mueller. While not listed below, many of Austin’s best breweries also host watch parties or have large screens for sports. For those looking to tailgate, scope out Austin’s best bets for tailgating with our complete guide to tailgating for UT Longhorn games . Eater.com Subscribe to Kangtown Facebook Twitter Instagram Youtube RSS Eater Eater logo Eater Bang Bang Is Headed to Austin Pop-Ups Eater Bang Bang Is Headed to Austin For one night only, Nixta Taqueria and Lao’d Bar are joining forces for a two-dinner-one-night feast by Eater Staff Aug 13, 2026, 10:55 PM UTC Facebook Link Eater’s Bang Bang dinner series is heading to Austin, bringing together two of the city’s most exciting restaurants under one roof for one night only. On August 19, Nixta Taqueria and Lao’d Bar will collaborate on a two-part, six-course dinner that gives diners a chance to explore Mexican and Laotian cooking back-to-back, through bold flavors, shared traditions, and personal storytelling. The evening will open with Chef Edgar Rico’s signature masa-driven cooking, including duck carnitas tacos and Denver steak aguachile. Chef Bob Somsith will follow with dishes inspired by the flavors of Laos, from shrimp ceviche with fried stuffed shrimp head to a fish laab tostada. And expect a delightful collaborative dessert showcasing the best of both restaurants. “I’ve always believed food is one of the best ways to tell your story,” says Bob Somsith at Lao’d Bar. “I’m excited to share the kitchen with Edgar and explore the common threads between Lao and Mexican cuisine. Different histories, different flavors, but the same belief that food has the power to bring people together.” Chef Rico from Nixta agrees. “Even though our cultures are oceans apart, they share so many of the same values: hospitality, honoring those who came before us, and creating flavor bombs that stop you in your tracks.” Tickets are selling out fast, so if you’re in Austin on August 19, get yours today . And download the Eater app to hear about more great events like this. See you at the Bang Bang. VIP Access to the World's Best Sports Events These days the best hotel perk is no longer the room or the spa. It's front-row seats and access to all-star players. By Matt Ortile October 17, 2026 Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story This past August the Waldorf Astoria New York turned its almost 10,000-square-foot Grand Ballroom into a full-size tennis court. Under glittering chandeliers, pros like Ben Shelton, Tommy Paul, Leylah Fernandez, and Maria Sakkari played showcase matches as spectators sipped from Champagne flutes. The event, which coincided with the US Open, hosted meet-and-greets and coaching sessions with ardent devotees, all of whom later checked in to the plush rooms upstairs. “It [felt] a little outrageous, incredibly glamorous, and completely right,” says Jamie Kerr, vice president of luxury marketing strategy at Hilton. “After all, the Grand Ballroom is where New York has always gathered to see and be seen.” Our annual Readers' Choice Awards winners have been announced! We loved poring over the results to find out what’s sticking with readers and spinning the data into a snapshot of the current moment in travel. Ahead: your manual for planning that next adventure. View the complete list of Readers’ Choice Award winners here . The congregation of athletic aficionados keen to connect with their idols and fellow fans is indicative of a wider trend. The sports-tourism market was estimated to be worth $1.16 trillion in 2025 and now makes up about 10 percent of the tourism economy itself. It's the perfect amalgam of travelers' growing pursuits of wellness, mental stimulation, and once-in-a-lifetime experiences on their journeys. Travelers want to do more than just catch a game; they want to get on the court with Grand Slam winners and cheer in the VIP grandstands at Formula 1 races—and increasingly, it's top hotels that are helping facilitate that kind of VIP access. Create your trip here North America Chevron United States Chevron New York Places to Stay My Favorite Airbnb: A Hudson Valley Retreat With a Creekside Hot Tub and Sauna Between its storybook interiors and proximity to small-town shops, farm stands, and cider orchards, this group-friendly stay is one of my favorite upstate discoveries. By Jessica Chapel October 17, 2026 Courtesy of Airbnb Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Getting 12 people to agree on a weekend away is an exercise in logistics. Someone wants to hike ; someone else would rather browse antique shops; a few people are already asking what’s for dinner. My ideal group getaway? One that leaves room for all of it, with a house you're excited to return to in between excursions. On a recent October weekend , my friends and I—a total of six couples—found that combination at Schoonmaker Retreat , tucked in the quaint Hudson Valley hamlet of High Falls. As a lifelong New Yorker , I’ve made plenty of trips to the Catskills and Hudson Valley, but High Falls, Rosendale, and Accord were towns I hadn’t yet gotten to know. Rosendale had been on my radar thanks to the introduction of Six Bells Countryside Inn , a delightfully whimsical, British-inspired hotel, and the surrounding area seemed ripe for a fall weekend of vintage shopping , cider tasting, and lots of leaf-peeping . We lucked into a real Goldilocks window, with timing just right for trees to stand ablaze with reds, yellows, and the last bits of green. The weather was crisp, but still sunny enough to sit outside for hours, from long orchard lunches to cozy s’more nights. The Schoonmaker Retreat is in Ulster County, which straddles the towns of Rosendale and Marbletown. With two separate houses, a rushing creek running through the grounds, and a sauna and a cedar barrel hot tub beside the water, the sprawling estate gave our group a place to gather (or rather, frolic) between outings. We arrived on a Friday, trickling in at different times before tackling the first order of business: choosing bedrooms . The property has two historic buildings—the main, more contemporary Schoonmaker House and the slightly smaller, rustic-chic, and creekside Coach House. The latter is the property’s original base, used as a fort used for Mr. Schoonmaker himself during the Revolutionary War. The Story Behind the Façade | Condé Nast Traveler Skip to main content Condé Nast Traveler Condé Nast Traveler Inspiration Destinations Places to Stay News & Advice Shopping RCA 2026 Plan Your Trip Search Newsletters Account Menu Menu Condé Nast Traveler Account Search Menu Menu Plan Your Trip Inspiration Chevron Destinations Chevron Places to Stay News & Advice Chevron Curated Escapes Shopping Chevron RCA 2026 MORE Cruise Video Women Who Travel Search Search Newsletters Menu Search Close North America Chevron United States Chevron New York Chevron New York News & Advice Why is the Plaza Hotel Closing? The Story Behind the Façade Restoring the hotel’s historic exterior will require more than just throwing up the scaffolding and calling in a team. By Timothy Latterner October 16, 2026 Getty Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Of the 700+ hotels in New York City , The Plaza Hotel stands apart. Surrounded by skyscrapers, the stout, eighteen-story building at the corner of 59th Street and 5th Avenue, just south of Central Park , is more of an icon in the cityscape than any of its super-tall neighbors could hope to be. It hosted The Beatles just before their breakthrough performance on The Ed Sullivan Show , welcomed F. Scott and Zelda Fitzgerald, inspired the eponymous Neil Simon play Plaza Suite , acted as a backdrop in Home Alone 2, and was the home of the fictional Eloise , the little girl who roamed its elegant halls. Now, nearly 120 years after it first opened, it’s shutting its doors—at least for a few years. The Plaza's façade and the interior of the hotel are registered landmarks, recognized by both the national and city government. Richard Mandelkorn Starting in 2027, the Plaza Hotel will embark on a four-year-long renovation of its marble façade. First designed by Henry Janeway Hardenbergh in 1907, the hotel’s base and lower levels are crafted from rusticated marble, with the upper levels being made from a polished, smooth marble exterior. Rusticated marble deteriorates more quickly when exposed to the elements, and can often need to be repaired and restored within twenty years. Coincidentally, the 2027 renovation comes just 19 years after the last major renovation to the hotel in 2008. Restoring the hotel’s façade will require more than just throwing up the scaffolding and calling in a team. The façade and the interior of the hotel are recognized as registered landmarks both nationally and by the city. The Landmarks Preservation Commission is working closely with the hotel to help with the restoration efforts and preserve the architectural beauty of the building. By Jessica Chapel and Caitlin Morton October 15, 2026 Getty Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story If there’s one thing that can make me fall in love with winter, it’s the thought of wandering around a European city with snow under my boots , twinkling lights overhead, and somewhere cozy to duck into when the temperature dips too low. I’m always chasing snow, whether that means clipping into my snowboard for a few days on a mountain or venturing somewhere that feels especially magical in the colder months—and Europe in particular has a way of making winter feel like something to celebrate. From Austria to Norway , winter transforms medieval streets into living storybooks beneath a fresh dusting of snow. Christmas markets turn historic squares into glittering wonderlands, and cozy cafés become an excellent excuse to linger over a rich hot chocolate or mulled wine while the world passes by. It's like stepping straight into your own magical snow globe. The appeal of these 15 cities extends well beyond December. Throughout the chilly season, head to Alpine towns framed by dramatic mountain peaks, indulge your adventurous side on a lesser-known arctic escape, or visit a grand European capital that feels more intimate after the summer crowds have dispersed. If you do visit after the holiday rush, you'll likely find more room to explore at your own pace. Consider this your invitation to trade the winter blues for European enchantment—snow-dusted rooftops, candlelit dinners, northern lights, and all. — Jessica Chapel Pinterest Unsplash Luxembourg City, Luxembourg Best for: Fairytale fortifications and festive Christmas markets Luxembourg City makes a compelling case for a winter getaway, with its UNESCO -listed Old Town, centuries-old fortifications, and dramatic valleys that feel even more magical in the colder months. From late November through early January, the annual Winterlights festival transforms the capital with Christmas markets, illuminated streets, live performances, and an ice-skating rink. Browse the chalets for local specialties like Gromperekichelcher (Luxembourgish potato fritters), before warming up with hot chocolate or mulled wine. That means you’ll want to pack with an eye toward color, structure, and pattern, especially when checking in to this landmark Four Seasons property , which is fresh off an expansive reimagining by Mexican architecture firm Huber. Stand Up! is an exhibition, curated by Yabu Pushelberg, in partnership with UNAIDS exploring LGBTQIA+ identity, activism, and resilience in response to HIV/AIDS through photography, cultural artifacts, and community gathering. The exhibition brings together archival and contemporary works that examine queer history across generations—from the sexual liberation movement of the 1960s and ‘70s in New York to the AIDS epidemic and the conversations shaping queer communities today. “HIV/AIDS affects everyone and touches society at large. It is not longer limited to gay men or historically marginalized communities.” - George Yabu and Glenn Pushelberg. The exhibition traces the social, political, and human history of the epidemic, highlighting the UN’s goal to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030 through public engagement and social mobilization. This approach shapes narratives, creating environments that are centered on the human experience. A Solid Foundation ‍ We build affiliates based on proven operational discipline and mutual trust. By collaborating with teams who understand our design language, share our international standards of practice, and already speak our shorthand, we ensure they can accurately interpret our work, protect documentation rigor, and manage clients locally while keeping our global standard intact. ‍ Drag Click to play What we've Done STUDIO SAVANH Studio Savanh is a multidisciplinary design practice based in Bangkok. Founded by Sam Khouvongsavanh, the studio merges international luxury discipline with a deeply personal connection to Southeast Asia. Anchored by Khouvongsavanh’s tenure directing global projects, Studio Savanh operates as a regional affiliate within the Yabu Pushelberg network, pairing strict operational governance with a distinct creative voice and approaching each project with clarity and resolve. Working across hospitality, residential, and retail environments, the studio fuses global rigor with an intimate understanding of regional culture, craft, and material language. Rejecting trend cycles and spectacle, Studio Savanh creates spaces defined by proportion, restraint, and layered expression, shaping environments that feel modern, rooted, and enduring. ‍ “My time at Yabu Pushelberg profoundly reshaped my path as a designer. George and Glenn have been guiding lights in both design and life. As I return to my cultural roots in Southeast Asia, it feels only natural to bring a piece of my heritage into the work we create here.” Founder | Sam Khouvongsavanh studiosavanh.com info@studiosavanh.com @studiosavanh HANABI ‍ Hanabi: Art and Artists curates intentional art collections that translate compelling stories into engaging, tactile experiences. The dining experience needed to move naturally from the open kitchen to the terrace, with an upper level that could shift between gathering and privacy without losing the energy of the room below. ‍ From open kitchen to open air ‍ We framed the interiors around Japanese and Greek influences both past and present. Influenced by the Rat Pack, Sammy Davis Jr., Silk Sonic, and cinematic music video lighting, The Pinky Ring offers a glimpse into Bruno Mars’s imagination, high on drama yet never flashy. Full Concept ‍ Our studio was entrusted by Bruno Mars to design the interiors, lighting, branding, and styling of this alluring establishment. As a conduit to his vivid imagination, our teams seamlessly translated his cinematic concepts into a fully sensorial experience. On Tour ‍ Guests are guided through a journey that begins with a circular screen façade, protecting them from the glare and sound of the casino. Upon entry, they are drawn into another world through a dimly lit mirrored passageway that features Bruno Mars’s Grammy Award collection. ‍ Inspired by contemporary museum design, we shaped the corridor as an exhibition space where guests can reset their visual palette after leaving the casino floor. At the heart of The Pinky Ring, a sunken conversation pit awaits, perfect for circling, socializing, seeing, and being seen. Perpetual Allure ‍ The design draws inspiration from music videos to make guests feel and look stage ready. We balanced low level contrast, and accent lighting to create a sultry ambiance. The most striking illumination appears in the VIP champagne room, where mirrors and simple sconces refract light to create layered reflections across the space. Realized Vision ‍ The Pinky Ring is both a metaphorical and literal reflection of Bruno Mars’ style, translated into a physical experience. A lavish venue with a star studded guest list, that balances glamour with substance. It has been featured in Wallpaper*, Dezeen, and was recognized as Interior Design’s Project of the Year. Innovation Within Heritage ‍ Founded in 2016, Muli is a China-based home systems brand that blends architecture-scale craftmanship with intelligent technology to elevate daily living. Muli asked for an environment that showcased its smart systems and integrated home solutions while honoring the cultural significance of the Qing Dynasty temple. ‍ They sought a space where contemporary technology blends seamlessly with restraint, supporting rather than overtaking the historic structure. The flagship showroom needed a residential quality that encourages a calm, exploratory experience rather than a typical retail visit. Good Bones ‍ Guided by spatial planning and material restraints, our team balanced the temple’s historic structure with contemporary design, allowing Muli’s home solutions to coexist naturally within centuries-old architecture. ‍ The original quadrangle courtyard, a defining element of classical Chinese architecture, is fully integrated as a spatial and emotional anchor, it connects the surrounding rooms with the ease and comfort of a lived-in home. Unified Interiors ‍ The interiors drew on our interdisciplinary practice, combining interior design, architectural design, lighting, art consultancy, and styling to create a residential experience within the historic temple. ‍ Working in tandem ensured that contemporary elements felt integrated rather than imposed, with each gesture balancing cultural depth and clarity. The nearly 2,000 square meter space welcomes approximately 370 Business Elite and Business Class guests, marking the airline's first premium airport lounge. ‍ Designed for Generosity ‍ Riyadh Air set out to create a lounge that moves beyond the conventions of the typology. Grounded in Hafawa and deeply rooted in Saudi culture, the space is defined by warmth and generosity, while expressing the airline’s technology-forward approach to restorative travel. ‍ The Desert as a Muse ‍ Yabu Pushelberg crafted a holistic design that unites interior architecture, industrial design, lighting, and wayfinding into a technology-forward sequence of spaces layered with tactility and precision. Inspired by wind-shaped desert dunes and the boundless skies above, each environment becomes a dialogue between earth and sky. Drawing from the Saudi landscape, the interiors explore a series of dualities: grounded yet ethereal, comforting yet technologically advanced. A restrained color palette, authentic materials, and textured finishes establish a calm, welcoming atmosphere. ‍ ‍ Light Leads The Way ‍ Light is integral to the experience. items.title: Our Commitments | Lore Group Hotels & Restaurants
items.text: Our Commitments | Lore Group Hotels & Restaurants About Us Our Hotels Design Meetings & Events Press Careers Gift Cards Plan Your Stay Newsletter Sign Up Become a Member Sign In Find Out More Close Become a Member Sign In Find Out More Book Now Book Now Our Commitments LORE GROUP SUSTAINABILITY MISSION STATEMENT Sustainability isn’t just actions, it’s attitude — and, for us, it’s an ongoing, transparent, measurable process of thinking responsibly and behaving ethically. We aim for the kind of commitment that cultivates a deeper connection with community and ensures all our social and environmental efforts are supported by auditable data. WHAT DO WE CARE ABOUT AND WHY? Lore Group is a family of independent hotels, bars and restaurants brought to life by people and place. Our businesses are inspired by their neighbourhoods, their communities, always intended to generate stories — of substance — that last. Storytelling, for us, is also about sharing the how and why, our hotels consider their connection to the bigger climate picture. Sustainability is a journey with no end point; we are always learning, evolving, adapting, and open to new ideas and innovations. We aim to follow-science-based frameworks and report every aspect of our impact — both negative and positive — quantitatively and qualitatively where relevant, always honestly and transparently. We try always to be fair-minded and inclusive and be generous of spirit, treating hotel guests with the warmth and consideration we would treat a guest in our own homes, and invite them to join us on our sustainability journey through our messaging. This is our way of articulating how our actions match our intentions, as we keep thinking of new ways to do better. LORE GROUPS EXTRA SMART GUIDE In a world where so much is now generated, we liked the idea of something altogether more human. Lore Group’s second ESG Report, handwritten by sustainability expert and Bouteco founder Juliet Kinsman, focuses on measurable impact, transparency and responsible design. It sets out our environmental, social and governance performance across all seven hotels, including both the progress we’ve made and the work still ahead. Submit 2026® Hotel St. Augustine 2025 Houston, TX Hotel, Food & Beverage Role Interior Design Scope New Construction: Interior Design-71 Guest Rooms, Lobby, Pool + Patio, Restaurants, Bars, Event Space Partners Client: Bunkhouse Group Architect: Lake Flato Landscape: Ten Eyck Lighting: Within Lighting Contractor: Forney Construction Photography: Nicole Franzen Project Narrative Introducing Hotel Saint Augustine, a collaboration with Bunkhouse Hotels and Lake Flato Architecture. Hotel Saint Augustine, a collaboration with Bunkhouse Hotels, is built on Houston’s esteemed Menil campus. The hotel’s design is a tribute to John and Dominique Menil’s personal collection, philosophy, and artistic community. Our design employs bold, saturated colors, reflective materials, and unexpected shapes to build an artful narrative . With a careful curation of vintage and custom pieces, the result is a playful yet refined destination for both visitors and locals to mingle, engage, and experience each space as their own. The lobby of Hotel Saint Augustine was designed to mimic a curator’s private home. Composed of adjacent open parlors and seating areas, its layout is conducive to various nooks for progressive gathering throughout the day. The rooms take cues from the De Menil’s own Houston home in River Oaks, designed by Philip Johnson with Interiors by Charles James. The custom sofas in the St. Augustine rooms are upholstered in a fabric inspired by the drawings of James and the tonal cabinets are a nod to the dressing rooms of the original house. Submit 2026® Sonoma Residence 2026 Sonoma, CA Residential Role Interior Design Scope Renovation and New Construction: Private Residence Partners Client: Andrew Mariani Architect: Robert Baumann Architects Landscape: Terremoto Project Narrative The house sits quietly behind vine and oak, a block from Sonoma’s square, its presence revealed only by a murmur of overgrowth. Built in 1847 by H.A. Green, the adobe has witnessed politics, imprisonment, and family life. That same year, John Nash was held here by Lt. William T. Sherman. Restored in 1931 by Zolita, it remains part of California’s layered history. Now the home is shaped around gathering—long dinners, wine, and fire. It is not solitary, but deeply communal. The adobe is its soul. Thick walls hold cool air; a long French table anchors the main room by the hearth. Worn floors, linen curtains, and deep-set windows carry the weight of time. Above, a raw attic becomes an unexpected wine parlor, softly lit and deliberately unfinished. A restrained modern wing extends the house, wrapping a quiet courtyard. Described as “California Monastic,” it favors simplicity—light, proportion, and craft over excess. The kitchen and living spaces follow suit: timeless cabinetry, elemental materials, and carefully chosen pieces meant to endure. Bedrooms unfold like small landscapes, each tied to courtyards and gardens. This is not architecture as spectacle, but something slower and more enduring—a conversation between adobe and air, fire and vine, and a family’s life within a landscape that remembers. items.title: Bio
items.text: Bio Inicio Bio Clientes Contacto Inicio Bio Clientes Contacto La velocidad para capturar la luz a través del tiempo... Desde muy joven, Oscar Mendoza , fotógrafo profesional originario de la Ciudad de México, descubrió su profunda conexión con las artes. A los 17 años, mientras exploraba la música y sus diversas tesituras para transmitir sentimientos, encontró en la fotografía su verdadera pasión, inclinándose especialmente por el ámbito comercial . Su formación en diseño gráfico complementó esta vocación, permitiéndole profesionalizar su arte. El talento de Oscar rápidamente se hizo evidente, y sus fotografías comenzaron a ser publicadas en reconocidos medios de comunicación como "Paréntesis" y "La Jornada". Esta trayectoria lo llevó a colaborar durante cuatro años en el prestigioso Laboratorio Mexicano de Imágenes (LMI) , una experiencia que consolidó su experticia en el campo. Con una sólida base y una visión clara, Oscar decidió emprender su camino como fotógrafo independiente . Desde entonces, ha forjado una impresionante cartera de clientes en el ramo de la fotografía de producto , colaborando con marcas de renombre internacional como Nike, Telcel, Pineda Covalín, La Mascota "Xico", Mezcal Lágrimas de Dolores, Uriarte Talavera, Palacio de Hierro y New Balance , entre otras. Su habilidad para destacar la esencia de cada producto lo ha convertido en un socio indispensable para estas empresas. La afición de Oscar por los automóviles también se ha traducido en una destacada carrera en la fotografía automotriz. Con más de 10 años de experiencia en este nicho, se ha posicionado como un referente en la industria, trabajando con clientes de la talla de Escudería Telmex (con el reconocido piloto Sergio Pérez), Corvette, Chevrolet, GAC, RTR, Shelby México, Nissan México, Ford y American Racing . Su maestría para capturar la velocidad, el diseño y la potencia de los vehículos es inigualable. Además, ha colaborado con Effi Muñíz, del popular programa de TV "Mexicánicos", consolidando aún más su reputación en este sector. Comprometido con el crecimiento de la comunidad fotográfica, Oscar también se ha desempeñado como docente , impartiendo cursos especializados en iluminación en diversas instituciones como Gym de Arte y Cultura, EduMac, Veintiún Milímetros y Nikon México. Actualmente, es miembro activo de NPS (Nikon Professional Service) y profesor de la especialidad en fotografía comercial en el Instituto IMAGO . items.title: Autos
items.text: Autos Inicio Bio Clientes Contacto Inicio Bio Clientes Contacto Autos La fotografía automotriz es la perfecta unión entre la pasión y la precisión. En esta sección, la velocidad, la potencia y el diseño se capturan con gran dedicación. Cada toma está pensada para resaltar las líneas, la aerodinámica y el carácter de los vehículos, desde la Escudería Telmex hasta un clásico 37s chevy. Más que solo autos, son obras de arte en movimiento, inmortalizadas a través de un lente con años de experiencia. items.title: 2025 in Review — Patrick Michael Chin
items.text: 2025 in Review — Patrick Michael Chin Home Projects Food & Beverage About 2025 in Review Learn from Me Contact Menu Home Projects Food & Beverage About 2025 in Review Learn from Me Contact As of December 2025, I’m stepping into my twelfth year of photography, and my gratitude still grows with every one. I went freelance in December of 2014, and I’m still pleasantly surprised, year after year, by where this path has led. I love making photographs more than ever, and I feel incredibly lucky to call this my job. So if you’ve ever shared my work, offered a kind word, assisted on a shoot, recommended me to someone, or trusted me enough to hire me… thank you. Truly. I had some incredibly special and fun projects this year that I’m excited to share, but more than any of the work itself, 2025 stands out as my favorite year yet at home and on the road with my family. I’m endlessly grateful that photography has given me the gift of experiencing new places alongside my wife and kiddos and if you make this to the bottom of this novel of a recap I had such a fun time collecting images together from a bucket list year in the Chin household. Thank you for taking a moment to look back with me and celebrate a few favorite projects and family moments from 2025. Once again this year, starting 2025 with a client like Bose was really unfair. I had so many incredible projects this year but to say any of them made me feel as giddy and “I’ve really made it” as Bose would be a lie. I was a small part in a probably 40-50+ person crew on this shoot but it’s such a thrill to be part of a large crew like this where everyone gets to really hyper-focus on their one thing. The creative and production was so strong on this shoot that it would honestly have been hard to make bad photos here, but I’m really proud of my small role in things here and I love the photos so much. I recall having a huge ear-to-ear grin on my face every time I would look back at the monitor at what we were getting throughout the three days on set because I just truly love these images and it’s exactly the type of thing I love doing most. More of this, please. Photographed in Los Angeles, CA. 2025 marked my second year of helping Oade with creative direction, photo, and my first foray into some video work as well! I deeply love what we get to work on with Oade - from shooting the people and places behind the farming, production, and bottling in France, to shooting with partners and collaborators in Napa, merch and e-comm work in my kitchen at home, as well as launch events around the country, it was a busy year and it shows. I love how expansive and rich in texture and place the images and videos feel. I’m looking forward to building this even more in 2026!
